name: Pendau
confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand descriptions agree (1 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed penultimate, no secondary stress, quantity-insensitive; penultimate stress) rests on the standard 750-page Pacific Linguistics reference grammar, which itself contains an acoustic F0 study of stress; the quotation is verbatim at sec. 2.7.1 pp. 50-51 and echoed at p. 23. The source was not yet obtained before; it is now saved under our check folder, so the blank grade/quote/loc fields can be filled (loc: PL 590, sec. 2.7.1 pp. 50-51; sec. 2.3 p. 23) and the cite relabelled from 'ANU thesis PDF' to 'Pacific Linguistics 590 (2007), ANU Open Research handle 1885/28970'. Optional refinement for the not yet coded domain: stress is post-lexical and counts suffixes and enclitics (pp. 35-36, 60, 98), i.e. domain = word plus enclitics. no reclassification.

sources.citation: Quick 2008, A Grammar of the Pendau Language, ANU thesis PDF (handle 1885/28970), sec. 2.3, 2.7.1
sources.quote: In Pendau, primary stress is predictable on the penultimate syllables of words, thus it is not phonemic (see the phonetic details in 2.6.2). There is no secondary stress [...] Pendau is not Quantity Sensitive.

sources.locator: §2.7.1 Metrical structure of stress in Pendau, printed pp. 50-51 (PDF the text); also §2.3 p. 23: 'Stress is always on the penultimate syllable and is unmarked…
sources.note: Catalog: fixed penultimate (penultimate stress), sec_status 'stated: none (one stress per word)', no-tone. The grammar states exactly this: penultimate primary stress, not phonemic, no secondary stress (fn. 29, p. 52: no evidence of a second L-H contour within a word; 'Primary stress is a cumulative prosody'), not quantity-sensitive, domain = phonological word including enclitics (stress assigned post-lexically; 'the enclitics receive penultimate stress and therefore are part of the phonological word', §3.3.4 pp. 61-62; epenthetic vowel in penultimate position takes stress, e.g. [junjung:onyo…

sources.citation: Quick, Phil. 2007. A grammar of the Pendau language of central Sulawesi, Indonesia. Pacific Linguistics 590. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, RSPAS, ANU. (ANU Open Research handle 1885/28970)
sources.quote: p. 50: 'In Pendau, primary stress is predictable on the penultimate syllables of words, thus it is not phonemic ... There is no secondary stress'; p. 51 rule 3: 'Pendau is not Quantity Sensitive'; p. 23: 'Stress is always on the penultimate syllable'; p. 98: 'Penultimate stress applies the same for enclitics and suffixes and applies to both post-lexically'; p. 35: penultimate stress moves onto the second half of a long vowel when an enclitic is added.

sources.locator: §2.7.1 Metrical Structure of Stress in Pendau, printed pp. 53-54; also §2.6.2.2, p. 46: 'The results from this analysis shows that the main phonetic realizatio…
sources.note: Rule (fixed penultimate, one stress per word), secondary status (none) and tone class (no-tone: the L-H pitch accent is explicitly non-phonemic, fn. 28 p. 46 contrasts it with Japanese-type lexical pitch accent) are confirmed verbatim. Refinements the catalog entry does not record: (a) weight: 'Pendau is not Quantity Sensitive' (p. 54), so heavy = none can be stated rather than left blank; (b) domain: stress is postlexical on the phonological word including enclitics, 'the movement of penultimate stress when there is the addition of an enclitic' (p. 37) and the grid examples nda'u / ndau'po 'n

sources.citation: Quick, Philip A. (2006). A lexicographical introduction and inventory of Pendau fish names.
sources.note: The work neither supports nor contradicts the catalog's penultimate-stress record; it contains no statement about stress at all. The Glottolog tag 'grammar sketch' is inaccurate for this item: it is a fish-name lexicon with some morphosyntactic notes on compounding, not a sketch with a phonology section.

sources.citation: Quick, Philip A. (2002). A sketch of the primary transitive verbs in Pendau. In The history and typology of western Austronesian voice systems. Canberra: Research School of Pacific and Asian Studies, Australian National University. pp. 101-22.
sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.locator: printed p. 102, section 2 'Nominal and verbal paradigms' and footnote 5
sources.note: Morphosyntax paper (nong-/ni- transitive verb forms, word order, applicatives, TAM, discourse pivots). The full text (22 PDF pages, pp. 101-122) has no occurrence of stress, accent, tone, penult, syllable, prosody, pitch or intonation, no stress diacritics in any example, and no phonology section. The only phonological remarks are the two quoted: clitic pronouns join the phonological word, and enclitics vs free words are told apart by unstated 'phonological criteria'. Nothing usable for the catalog stress rule (fixed penultimate, from Quick 2007) or the no-tone class.
sources.venue: The history and typology of western Austronesian voice systems
